stem: A public Claude-powered writing assistant pre-screens every request with a lightweight classifier and refuses flagged ones. Logs show that a few accounts submit hundreds of reworded jailbreak attempts each day, probing until one slips through. What should the team add?

options.text: Loosen the classifier threshold so fewer requests are flagged and these accounts have less feedback to learn from.
options.why: Weakening the screen lets more attacks through for everyone; it trades a real control for less visibility.

options.text: Track refusals per account, warn accounts that repeatedly trigger them, and throttle or suspend persistent offenders.
options.why: Responding to repeat offenders is a recommended jailbreak mitigation: persistent probing is tied to an identity, and throttling or banning removes the attacker's unlimited retries.

options.text: Replace the refusal message with a normal-looking answer so attackers cannot tell that their attempt was blocked.
options.why: Deceptive responses confuse legitimate users who were misclassified and do nothing to stop an account from continuing to probe.

options.text: Route these accounts to a larger model tier, since it follows the system prompt more reliably under pressure.
options.why: Model size is not an access control; the accounts keep unlimited attempts, and a capable model can still be manipulated.

explanation: Jailbreak defense is layered: screen inputs, harden the system prompt, and respond to repeat offenders. When the same account repeatedly triggers refusals, tell the user the behavior violates the usage policy and throttle or ban them, so an attacker cannot keep iterating until one attempt succeeds.
reference: Claude API docs — Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections

stem: An agent reads inbound customer emails through a get_email tool and drafts replies. The developer currently concatenates each email body into a plain-text tool result, followed by a line of processing instructions for Claude. Which two changes follow the recommended handling of this untrusted content? (Choose two.)

options.text: Return the email as a JSON object (source, sender, subject, body) so the body is an escaped string, not free text.
options.why: JSON encoding gives unambiguous delimiters, so text inside the body cannot close a quote or tag and break out into an instruction context.

options.text: Pass each email body to a lightweight classifier and return a stripped summary instead if injection is suspected.
options.why: Screening tool output with a small, schema-constrained classifier before it becomes a tool_result catches many injections before Claude acts on them.

options.text: Keep the processing instructions inside the tool result, next to the email, so Claude sees them in the same place.
options.why: Claude treats tool-result content as untrusted, so your own instructions there may be ignored or flagged; send them in a user turn after the tool_result instead.

options.text: Move the email body into the system prompt so Claude reads it with the same care as its standing instructions.
options.why: The system prompt is the most trusted channel; placing third-party text there gives injected instructions maximum authority.

options.text: Surround the body with a custom marker such as ===END EMAIL=== and tell Claude to ignore anything after it.
options.why: An attacker can simply include the same marker in the email; ad hoc delimiters in free text do not create a reliable boundary.

explanation: Deliver third-party content only in tool_result blocks, label its source, JSON-encode untrusted strings so they cannot break out of the data context, and screen tool output before Claude acts on it. Keep your own instructions out of tool results and out of the same channel as untrusted data, and never elevate that data into the system prompt.
reference: Claude API docs — Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections

stem: A team is about to launch an agent that reads vendor invoices from email and can create payment requests. Its guardrails include tool-output screening, a system-prompt policy on untrusted content, and human approval above a set amount. Which step best verifies these guardrails before and after launch?

options.text: Run the eval suite of normal invoices and ship once accuracy on extraction meets the target threshold.
options.why: Happy-path evals measure task quality, not whether guardrails hold against adversarial content.

options.text: Rely on Claude's built-in resistance to prompt injection, since the model is trained to be skeptical of tool results.
options.why: Built-in resilience is one layer; the application's own screens and approvals still need to be tested against attacks.

options.text: Red-team with invoices that carry injection attempts, confirm each layer catches them, then monitor live outputs.
options.why: Adversarial testing shows whether the screens and approval steps actually stop attacks, and continuous monitoring catches new techniques after launch.

options.text: Launch to all users at once and add further guardrails only after users report an incident in production.
options.why: Waiting for incidents means the first successful injection causes real payments before anything is learned.

explanation: Safe deployment means validating guardrails, not just listing them. Before launch, red-team the workflow with documents, emails and tool outputs that contain deliberate injection attempts and confirm the screening and confirmation steps catch them; after launch, continuously monitor outputs for signs of successful injection and refine the controls.
reference: Claude API docs — Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections

stem: A company runs a two-day internal hackathon where 40 employees need Claude API access. Security wants the credentials to stop working automatically afterward and the event's spend kept separate and capped. How should access be provisioned?

options.text: Share one production key with all participants and rotate it manually once the hackathon has finished.
options.why: Sharing a production key exposes production, prevents attribution, and depends on someone remembering to rotate it.

options.text: Create never-expiring keys in the Default Workspace and ask participants to delete their own keys afterward.
options.why: Relying on participants to clean up leaves live credentials behind, and usage mixes with the rest of the organization.

options.text: Have each person create a personal key in a capped hackathon workspace, expiring when the event ends.
options.why: Expiration makes keys stop working without manual cleanup, per-person keys keep usage attributable, and the workspace isolates and caps spend.

options.text: Create one hackathon key and paste it into the event's shared channel so anyone can pick it up when needed.
options.why: Posting a key in a channel spreads it beyond the intended audience and gives no per-person attribution or revocation.

explanation: Match credential lifetime and scope to the need. Temporary access should use keys created with an expiration (it cannot be added later), issued per person for attribution, in a dedicated workspace with its own spend limit so the event is isolated from production and capped.
